stops.name: Pelrapeire (Montpellier), the starving city
stops.campa: Riding the road from Graharz, Parzival comes on Pelrapeire under siege, its granaries emptied, its young queen Condwiramurs pressed by an unwanted suitor, Clamide, whose seneschal Kingrun has starved the town toward surrender. The gate opens to the unknown Red Knight more from desperation than hope. Condwiramurs herself, though a queen ruling alone, comes to his chamber that first night only to weep and ask his help, and lies beside him chastely till dawn, for Parzival, new to love as to everything else, does not yet know what more a wife might ask of a husband.

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the duels with Kingrun and Clamide
stops.campa: Parzival rides out and unhorses the seneschal Kingrun in single combat, then, when Clamide himself arrives with his army, defeats the king as well, in each case sparing the beaten man's life exactly as Gurnemanz taught him and sending him instead to surrender himself at Arthur's court in Bertane. The besieging host, leaderless, withdraws. Pelrapeire's granaries fill again from the countryside; the city that had been eating its last stores now feasts its deliverer, and Condwiramurs, who has watched her fate decided twice in a single day by a boy barely a knight, begins for the first time to hope.

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the marriage of Condwiramurs
stops.campa: With the siege broken, Condwiramurs and Parzival marry, and here too he learns from Kyot, Willehalm of Toulouse and Orange retired to his hunting lodge at Le Verdus, uncle to the queen and to Parzival's own dead mother's line, the man who found the Grail family in the forest behind Arlesheim twenty years before and married its first bearer, Schoysiane. Under Kyot's tutelage and his wife's rule Parzival passes more than a year at Pelrapeire, a husband and a king by marriage, still ignorant that the greatest test of his life, and his family's, waits a few months' ride to the north.

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the departure in search of his mother
stops.campa: Word of Herzeloyde's death has never reached her son. Restless after more than a year of settled rule, and troubled by a wish to know how his mother fares, Parzival asks his wife's leave to ride out, promising to return; she is left carrying his child. He rides north out of Pelrapeire not knowing the direction holds no news of a mother fourteen months dead, but a lake, a wounded king, and a question he has been unknowingly rehearsed since infancy to fail to ask.
stops.quote: And see how my mother fareth, if weal be her lot, or woe.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Lake Brumbane (Öleweiher), the fisher-king
stops.campa: After an enormous ride whose length he never afterward accounts for, Parzival comes at dusk on the nineteenth of September to a still fishing-lake in a valley he does not recognize, hemmed by rock on every side. A richly dressed man sits fishing from a boat, too sick to stand or ride, and directs the stranger to a castle he says is the only lodging for many miles. Parzival cannot see it from the water; only on climbing the far bank does Munsalvaesche appear above him, turreted, waiting, as if it had been built for this one evening alone.

stops.name: Munsalvaesche (Hornikopf), the bleeding lance and the Grail procession
stops.campa: In the great round hall of Munsalvaesche, built as if turned on a lathe, four hundred knights sit at their meal beside the ailing king Anfortas, who is the fisherman from the lake. A squire runs weeping through the hall bearing a lance from whose steel point blood runs unceasing down into his sleeve, and every man there groans aloud at the sight, though none will say why. Then in solemn procession enter maidens bearing golden vessels, silver knives, candles, and last a maiden crowned above the rest carrying on green silk the thing men call the Grail, root and flower of Paradise, which alone feeds the entire hall.
stops.quote: A squire sprang swift thro' the doorway, and a lance in his hand he bore... from the point did the blood run fast adown to the hand of the holder till 'twas lost in his sleeve at last... and then thro' the lofty palace was weeping and wailing sore.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, the silence and the sword
stops.campa: Watching the wonders of the hall and his grieving host, Parzival remembers only that Gurnemanz forbade him to ask too freely, and reasons that if he simply waits, someone will explain unasked how it stands here with this folk. Anfortas, in silent thanks that this stranger has not shamed him, presses into his hands a fine sword he can no longer wield himself. Parzival's fingers close on the hilt, the very moment, Wolfram says, when his silence might still have been broken; he says nothing. The Grail is borne out again. The feast ends. He is shown to bed unquestioned and unquestioning.
stops.quote: And he thought, 'Gurnemanz he bade me, in truth, without thought of guile, to withhold my lips from question. If here I abide awhile, methinks it will then befall me, as aforetime in Graharz land, they will tell me, without my question, how here with this folk it stands.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, the empty castle at dawn
stops.campa: He wakes to a castle stripped of every soul, his armor set ready by unseen hands, his horse saddled and waiting in an empty courtyard hung with silence where four hundred knights supped the night before. As he rides out, the drawbridge is hauled up so sharply behind him that his horse's hindquarters are nearly caught, and a voice curses him from a window, sun of the goose, for a fool who let his chance walk past him unspoken. He rides into the forest not yet understanding what door has just been shut, or that it will take him six years to find its hinge again.

stops.name: South foot of Birseck, Sigune weeping a second time
stops.campa: Riding down from the castle hill he cannot find again by looking back, Parzival comes on Sigune once more, seated now aloft in a linden tree with dead Schionatulander embalmed between her white arms, her brown hair shorn away for grief. She asks eagerly whether he asked the question at Munsalvaesche, the question that would have healed her uncle Anfortas and crowned him king of the Grail. He answers that he asked nothing. She curses him outright, dishonored and accursed, and will not speak to him again; he rides from her more wretched than any battle has left him.
stops.quote: Then he quoth, 'Nay, I asked no question!' 'Alas!' cried the mournful maid, 'that ever mine eyes have seen thee, who to question wast sore afraid... Thou hast seen the knives of silver, thou the bleeding spear hast seen. Alas! wherefore hast thou sought me? Dishonoured, accurst art thou.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Orilus Rock and the grotto of Proserpina, Jeschute vindicated
stops.campa: At the northern rock wall that marks the border of Soltane Forest, Parzival meets Jeschute again, still riding in the torn and shamed state Orilus imposed on her for the theft of a kiss she never invited. Duke Orilus, coming on them, attacks the stranger in fury, and this time Parzival unhorses him outright, then does what he could not do at Bromhübel: swears in a nearby cave, the grotto later called Trevrizent's, that Jeschute is and has always been innocent. Orilus, humbled, is reconciled to his wife. From the grotto's keeper Parzival takes up the spear of the knight Taurian to replace the one broken in the fight.

stops.name: Stollenrain, the three drops of blood in the snow
stops.campa: A hot day turns suddenly bitter overnight; snow falls thick over the ground between Arlesheim and Dornachbrugg. At dawn a falcon of King Arthur's, hunting wild geese, strikes one down; three drops of its blood fall glowing on the white snow at Stollenrain. Parzival, riding by, is transfixed at the sight: the red on white calls up his wife Condwiramurs's face so exactly that he falls into a waking trance, lance couched but unmoving, oblivious to the world, until a passing knight of Arthur's nearby camp spots the strange, motionless Red Knight and rides to report the wonder.
stops.quote: He thought, 'Say what hand hath painted these colours that here I see? Kondwiramur, I think well, these tints sure shall liken thee!'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: The Round Table camp on the Plimizoel (the Birs)
stops.campa: Arthur's whole court is camped along the river Wolfram calls the Plimizoel, the Birs, from Dornachbrugg to Münchenstein, tents pitched for a Round Table held in the field. Two knights ride out to challenge the entranced Red Knight and are unhorsed without his ever quite waking, until Gawain, gentler than the rest, approaches on foot, throws a silk cloth over the blood-drops to break the trance, and leads the bewildered Parzival back to camp as a guest. There, before Arthur and Guinevere, he is at last named a companion of the Round Table, the honor he set out from Soltane a year and a half before to win.
